Growing Baby Spinach (Spinacia oleracea) 
Using Simulated Lunar Regolith, Aquaculture Waste Products, and Hydrogel Beads 
 
Angie Barrutia, Olivia Enyart, Yehuda Leib Mahr, Hattie Ruff 
Postville High School 
Plant the Moon Challenge 
Experiment Time Period: February 16 - April 2, 2026 
 
 
 
Team Name: SmellsFishy1! 
Challenge Category: High School 
Team number: 25140

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 2 
Abstract 
This study explores the effects of fish-based organic fertilizer on the growth and harvest of baby 
spinach (Spinacia oleracea) as well as using hydrobeads as a water and nutrient source. Rainbow 
trout fish tailings were used to evaluate the effect of using fish waste products under different 
soil conditions. Plant growth was assessed by measuring leaf development, plant height, leaf size 
in length, and harvested wet mass. It was hypothesised that the use of organic fish matter, in the 
presence of hydrogel beads, would enhance plant growth and increase the production of edible 
leaves. Results indicate that using fish tailings may be an effective nutrient source for growing 
plants in simulated lunar regolith. Additionally, supplementing lunar regolith with hydrogel 
beads, and supplemental waterings with nutrient rich fish water also contributes to plant growth. 
The findings of this study suggests that more research using fish tailings, hydrogel beads, and 
nutrient rich fish water should occur. The results of this research could contribute to more 
sustainable and efficient agricultural practices in space and on earth. 
 
Background 
 
In the future, astronauts will require reliable and sustainable protein sources to support 
long-term life in space. Establishing a basic agricultural system will be essential for these 
missions. One proposed method involves vertical farming using baby spinach (Spinacia 
oleracea), which maximizes space efficiency, increases edible crop yield, and uses fish waste as 
a fertilizer. The cultivation of fish, such as tilapia, provides a rapid and efficient source of animal 
protein. A three-ounce serving of tilapia (3.9 ounces pre-cooked) contains 23 grams of protein, 
making it a highly nutritious option(Lui, 2020). In addition to providing protein, tilapia generates

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 3 
by-products such as fish emulsions (fertilizer derived from fish scraps), fish tailings, and 
nutrient-rich wastewater. 
Tailings consist of the sediment, extra food, and fish waste that settle to the bottom and 
ends (tails) of the fish runs during production. The organic fish matter and the nutrient rich 
water, have the potential to improve infertile environments, such as lunar soil. However, fish 
tailings, or “sludge”, is dense, slimy, and prone to compaction. This compaction could be 
reduced by adding lunar regolith. 
Moon regalith contains agglutinates, a mineral fragment that takes up to 60% - 70% of 
materials (Noble, 2019). Agglutinates do not contain nutrients. Plants need P,N,K (phosphorus, 
nitrogen, and potassium) to grow. The use of the fish tailings and fish water provide nutrients to 
the plants, while the hydrogel beads store these nutrients, making them easily accessible to the 
plants. 
The moon regolith does not have microorganisms. Microorganisms improve the root 
growth and development of plants. The addition of microorganisms to regalith has been 
demonstrated to enhance plant growth (Ameha, S. et al., 2025). Fish water and tailings may 
provide additional microbes that could enhance plant growth. The addition of topsoil would 
improve growth medium quality, add microbial life, and reduce compaction, all which are 
critical for root development. The topsoil used in this experiment was collected from rodent 
mounds located at the edge of agricultural fields located in Chickasaw County, Iowa. 
It was hypothesized that the use of the nutrient filled hydrogel beads would feed the 
plants and direct the roots for better nutrient and water absorption. Additionally, the utilization 
of the hydrogel beads would provide space for the roots to grow. The use of the central tube

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 4 
would provide a constant nutrient/water source, keeping the beads hydrated. The use of 
aquarium air pumps will saturate the water and soil with oxygen. 
The Spayberry STEM Moon Explorers 1 demonstrated that the use of hydrogels 
showed promise for directing root growth (Yacob, F., 2025). This experiment was to explore 
the effectiveness of hydrobeads as a source of nutrients delivery and seed starting medium. 
The advantage of hydrogel beads are very small and do not expand until hydrated. Because of 
this, the hydrogel beads have a reduced shipping volume, and they can be hydrated at their 
final location. Both of wich are important considerations in space transport. 
 
Discussion of Variables 
The aim of this project was to determine what effect, if any, growing baby spinach 
(Spinacia oleracea) with organic fertilizer derived from fish waste has on plant growth and 
usable food production. The hypothesis was that the addition of fish-based organic matter and the 
use of hydrobeads would enhance plant growth and increase the yield of edible baby spinach 
(Spinacia oleracea) leaves. 
The independent variables are changed to observe their effect on plant growth. In this 
experiment, the independent variables were soil composition and water source. Fish tailings 
were obtained through Iowa DNR employee Chuck Gipp at the Decorah Fish Hatchery rainbow 
trout rearing station in Decorah, Iowa . Water was either distilled water or water obtained from 
school fish tanks. 
The dependent variables, which were measured to determine the outcome of the 
experiment, included leaf growth, plant height and leaf size, wet mass of harvested leaves, root,

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 5 
and shoot mass. These measurements provided data on both above-ground and below-ground 
development of the baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) plants. 
Control variables were kept consistent throughout the experiment to ensure accurate 
results. Some controlled variables were: seed type, temperature, watering schedule, moisture 
content, planter types, and where the fish tailings and fish water came from. The purpose of 
controlling variables is to isolate the effects of the independent variables on the growth and 
development of the plants. 
 
Experimental Design Explanation 
Microscopic analysis of lunar regolith 
revealed small crystalline structures that could 
potentially damage young plant roots. When 
water was introduced, these particles formed a 
dense, compacted sludge, further highlighting 
the challenges of growing plants in such an 
environment. 
Based on these observations, Spinacia oleracea seeds were germinated 
using two different methods: the paper towel method and the hydrogel method. 
The paper towel method was intended to better prepare seedlings for harsh soil 
conditions, while the hydrogel method provided an alternative germination 
environment that encapsulated the seed in a protective covering. 
For the paper towel method, Hillyard brand biodegradable paper towels were moistened

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 6 
and folded around the seeds before being placed in resealable plastic ziplock 
bags with airflow. These were kept in a greenhouse on heating pads set to 
72°F (22.2°C). Similarly, seeds placed in hydrated hydrogels were inserted 
using a bent tweezer, placed in ziplock bags, and then stored under the same 
conditions. In addition to baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) , beets, 
cucumbers, and mint were planted in both the hydrogel beads and paper 
towels. 
After day one, seed expansion was observed in both methods. By the 
second day, seedlings had begun to sprout in the paper towel method, while 
the hydrogels showed only continued swelling. Growth in the hydrogels did 
not progress further for any species, however, the paper towel method 
produced viable seedlings with significant root growth for all sampled plants. 
Baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) was selected for our test species. Seeds were started 
again using the paper towel method. After three days on the heat mat, 
the new seedlings were transplanted into soil mixtures, with four 
seedlings placed into each of seven growth tubes. Each growth tube had 
4 holes that were labeled A, B, C, and D. 
The growth tubes were constructed from 4" x 4" x 3" PVC 
Y-connectors allowing for growth vertically. The base was sealed with a 
4” cap, and 17cm 3” diameter pipe extension was added with a 3” cap. 
Four holes were drilled into each tube extension to house the seedlings, each being named A,B, 
C, and D. This made documenting information easier and more

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 7 
efficient. 
Each system used either distilled water or nutrient-rich fish water. An aquarium air pump 
was used to maintain oxygen and nutrient circulation. A cellulose sponge was placed at the base 
of the 17cm tube to prevent soil from entering the water reservoir while still allowing for water 
absorption. Cellulose is made of wood pulp, making it a fast biodegradable option. Plants were 
watered once a day by filling the middle pipe to the top of the ‘y hole’. With the added 
hydrobeads, extra moisture was absorbed. The idea was to prevent plants from being drowned. 
In cases of high moisture, the supplemental greenhouse fan was turned on. The hydrobeads were 
also used to help guide plant root growth, which could grow into the sponge or up towards the 
tube cap. 
The tip of each root has a root cap. Inside it are special cells containing tiny, heavy 
starch-filled statoliths. When gravity pulls on them, the statoliths sink to the bottom of the 
cell—like a built-in level. As a result, the root curves downward. In microgravity, water forms 
floating blobs, making it easier for plants to dry out—or drown—at the same time. Oxygen 
diffusion to roots is reduced and the plant begins to suffer (Cowing, 2025). By using the 
hydrobeads to guide the roots, and the aquarium air pump to provide extra oxygen, plants were 
allowed sufficient water intake and were nutrient sufficient. 
Various soil compositions were tested, including combinations of lunar regolith, Earth 
soil, fish tailings, straw manure, and hydrobeads. Control groups used only Earth soil, while 
experimental groups incorporated regolith and other organic matter. The systems were watered 
with either distilled water or nutrient rich fish water to evaluate the effects of different fertilizer 
sources.

amount of each additive was used.

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 9 
Once transplanted, the seedlings were monitored closely and moisture was kept at a 
constant. After one week, the cotyledons, the seed leaves, were removed to encourage the plants 
to direct energy toward true leaf development and vertical growth. Cotyledons are not considered 
part of the mature plant structure, but serve as early nutrient sources during germination 
(“Cotyledon.” Encyclopaedia Britannica). 
 
During the growth period, multiple replantings took place in nearly every experiment 
version besides Earth 1 and Experiment 2. Four days after the initial transplant, Moon Control A, 
B, C, and D were replanted. Throughout the growth period, Earth 2 experienced one replanting 
of one plant, Earth 3 experienced one replant of one plant, Experiment 1 experienced one 
replanting of one plant, and Experiment 3 experienced one replant of three plants. 
 
Midway through the experiment, it was noted that the baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) 
had grown its reproductive system and few plants had actually grown seeds that were beginning 
to mature. These seeds were infertile, however, as hybrid seeds from ‘BURPEE’S’ were used. In 
future experiments, seeds from Seed Savers Exchange (seedsavers.org) will be used to ensure 
seed viability and seeds for future plantings. 
The cellulose sponges decomposed more quickly than what was anticipated. Future 
experiments should use thicker sponges or sponges made of material that will not deteriorate. 
On day 26, there were three plant losses in experiment #2 due to sponge deterioration and loss 
of soil into the water pipe.. The sponge was replaced with a 40-mm thick, rigid, foam substrate 
scrub sponge to maintain plant life for the continuation of Experiment 2 and other groups which 
showed signs of soil in the water. When exploring the sponges after the growth period, we found 
that the sponges decomposing at the quickest rate were the ones that contained the nutrient rich

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 10 
fish water. It is hypothesized that the fish water contained bacteria and other microbes which 
broke down the sponge much faster than the distilled water. 
Earth Control 3 was 100% earth soil. Moon Control was 100% simulated earth regolith. 
All experimental groups performed better than the Moon Control Group. Experimental group 
#2, using lunar regolith, fish water Hydrobeads, and watered daily with fish water showed more 
growth in height (Graph 1) and mass (Graph 2) than Earth Control 3 . Experiments 1 and 3 
performed better than the other two control groups for average height. Experiment 1 (fish 
tailings, DI water Hydrogel beads, and watered with DI water) had comparable mass to Earth 
Control 3.

In the final stages of the experiment, the above-ground portions of the plants were cut at 
ground level and weighed for the wet weight, and after dehydrating, a dry weight which was not 
applicable due to unmeasurable weights. Larger plants like basil could be used in future 
experiments to allow for usable dry weights. 
Roots were carefully removed from the soil for measuring and wet mass weighing using a 
gentle washing process which included soaking in a small tub and carefully maneuvering the 
tube to get the soil and roots out without harm. Later, they were taken for a more thorough wash 
using a turkey baster.

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 12 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Graph 5. Shows the average size of each leaf for each of the trials during the experiment. A drop in leaf 
size can indicate that more new plants were present. 
It was observed that the roots would grow into the cellulose sponges. When removing the 
solid compositions of plant soil from the tubes, root growths were found with Experiment 2 
having grown into the sponge. Experiment 2 showed accelerated growth after 3/22 (Graph 3). 
This suggests that the roots started using nutrient rich fishwater directly from this point forward. 
The results above imply that fish tailings and a combination of hydrobeads significantly 
improved plant growth and productivity of baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) in simulated lunar 
regolith over the length of the 45 day growth period.

GROWING BABY SPINACH (SPINACIA OLERACEA) 
 Barrutia, Enyart, Leib Mahr, Ruff 13 
 
Conclusion 
 The results of the experiment strongly supports the hypothesis that the addition of 
fish-based organic matter and the use of hydrobeads will enhance plant growth and increase the 
yield of edible baby spinach (Spinacia oleracea) leaves. Compared to the control group in 
standard earth soil, experiments using fish tailings and nutrient rich fish water showed 
comparable or greater growth patterns. This information indicates that these methods can help 
overcome the problem of infertile soil in space travel. 
 
This experiment introduced us to challenges such as the durability of the materials used 
as well as system stability when using cellulose sponges in nutrient-rich environments. In future 
experiments, sponge types could be adjusted for durability and control of soil moisture. 
Replacing the cellulose sponges with an artificial sponge would be more efficient for long-term 
use. Additionally, growing the control groups in pots, along with growth in the experimental 
setup can help determine the impact of the new planting strategy. Structural improvement will 
be taken into consideration for any future projects involving similar materials. 
These seeds produced in this experiment were infertile due to using hybrid plants. In 
future experiments, seeds from Seed Savers Exchange (seedsavers.org) will be used to ensure 
seed viability, seed purity, and producing seeds for future plantings. Despite limitations, this 
experiment was successful in suggesting that aquaculture waste products and unique watering 
techniques could play a key role in producing food in space using lunar regolith.
